name: Flat Vector Explainer
description: Bright, friendly vector illustration with no outlines: round chunky shapes filled with smooth gradients, crisp crescent shading and soft glows on a calm coloured backdrop, like a polished science channel animation.
suits: Good for science, tech and how-it-works topics told in a warm, approachable tone; less suited to grave, historical or luxury subjects that need texture or gravitas.
look: Backdrop is a wide two- or three-stop diagonal gradient in one cool hue family, with two or three huge, very faint radial glows that keep it from looking flat
Every object is built from simple geometric primitives (circles, capsules, rounded rectangles) with no stroke at all; edges come only from the fill against the backdrop
Each shape carries a linear gradient from a light tint at the lit side to a deep shade on the far side, with the light always coming from the upper left
Shading is done with one or two hard-edged crescents of a darker tone hugging the shadow side, plus a thin pale crescent rim on the lit edge; no soft airbrush
Small decorative sparkles: four-point stars made of pinched curves, scattered sparingly and twinkling, plus tiny dots of light
Depth comes from layering: big blurry-free background shapes in muted versions of the palette, mid-ground props, and a bright saturated foreground subject
Labels sit in white capsule pills with a soft dark drop shadow beneath and a faint glossy highlight strip along the top; an optional small pointer triangle aims at the subject
Headings are heavy rounded sans-serif in white, with a short dark offset shadow down and to the right to lift them off the backdrop
finish: Fine moving monochrome grain laid over everything in overlay mode, very light (around 8 to 10 percent), re-offset every frame so gradients never band
A second, static, large-scale soft mottle in overlay at about 10 to 12 percent so big gradient areas feel printed rather than digital
Soft radial glow sprites behind key objects (lamps, active elements, the key number), pulsing slowly by about 15 percent
motion: Everything eases in and out, and arrivals pop with a gentle overshoot: scale from zero past full size by about 10 percent, then settle
Idle objects never freeze: they bob a few pixels on a slow sine and their glows breathe
The camera does the storytelling: smooth push-ins and long pull-backs through scale, with background layers moving slower than foreground (parallax)
Scene changes are a large foreground shape sweeping across the whole frame as a wipe, or a dive into a glowing object that whites out and opens onto the next scene
Pace is lively but readable: a new element every one to two seconds, each landing on a beat
explaining: Arrows are thick rounded curves, often dotted with round dots, drawn on from tail to head, ending in a small rounded triangular head
Labels are white pills that pop in under or beside the thing they name, sometimes with a pointer
Key numbers are very large heavy rounded figures in white or yellow that count up quickly and then settle with a small bounce
Progress and comparison use fat rounded bars or ring gauges with a pale track and a bright gradient fill that grows
Right and wrong are shown with round badges (green check, red cross) that pop on, plus a brief coloured flash of the frame edge
Steps in a cycle are laid out as pills around a dotted loop with a travelling glowing dot showing the flow
sound: Soft marimba-like plucks for elements landing, in a calm minor-leaning key
Cute rounded boops that bend upward for small things popping in
Airy filtered-noise breaths for camera moves and wipes, with a warm low pad underneath
A warm low boom and bright chord on the key number
avoid: Outlines, ink strokes or sketchy edges on shapes
Photographic textures, realistic lighting or soft airbrushed shading in place of the hard crescents
Thin, light-weight or serif fonts
Muddy or desaturated colour; everything should feel clean and candy-bright against the deep backdrop

name: Watercolour Bloom
description: A hand-painted sketchbook page: see-through watercolour washes with dark dried rims, soft colour bleeds and blooms, grainy pigment and bare white paper for the highlights, over a light pencil drawing.
suits: Good for gentle, human, nature, wellbeing and storytelling topics with a calm reflective tone; weaker for dense data, hard-edged technical diagrams or urgent high-energy messages.
look: Surface is warm off-white cold-press paper with visible tooth: a fine bumpy height texture that also catches pigment, slightly warmer and darker toward the sheet edges
Every coloured area is a stack of many very transparent, irregular blobs: each blob is a polygon whose edges are jaggedly subdivided and jittered, so the edge is ragged, never a clean curve
Where a wash stops, pigment collects into a thin darker rim, while the middle stays lighter and uneven
Second colours are dropped into still-damp areas as soft fuzzy blooms that tint only inside the existing wash; some areas show a pale cauliflower-shaped back-run with a frilly edge
Highlights are not painted: they are left as bare paper, often a crescent or broken stroke with a crisp edge on one side
A faint grey pencil underdrawing shows around shapes: loose construction lines, slight overshoots, guide lines under lettering
Darker accents and contours are a few loose round-brush strokes on the shadow side only, tapering at both ends; a light splatter of small droplets near key subjects
Lettering is hand brushed, slightly uneven in weight and baseline, with the same darker pooled rim as the washes
finish: Every wash is composited onto the paper with multiply, never plain over, so overlaps darken like real glazes
Edge pooling on every wash: subtract a blurred copy of the wash alpha from itself and add the difference back, strongly enough that the rim reads clearly darker than the body
Granulation: pigment is boosted in the low points of the paper tooth, a speckled darkening of roughly 10 to 20 percent inside washes
Pigment load mottle: a soft low-frequency noise varies wash opacity by about half, so no area is an even flat tint
Paper tooth lighting baked into the whole frame at low strength, with a very soft warm vignette
motion: The pencil outline appears first, then each wash floods outward from its centre to fill it, over about half a second to a second
As a wash settles its rim darkens and any bloom slowly creeps outward, as if the water is drying
Brush strokes draw on along their path with a tapered head; titles are brushed word by word
The whole explainer lives on one long sheet: scene changes are slow camera pans along the paper to the next painted area
Pace is unhurried and calm; holds are a little longer than usual so the washes can be read
explaining: Each arrow is one full-bodied brush stroke: a ribbon that is thick at the start, thins along the way, with a darker pooled edge and a brushed arrowhead
Labels and counters are brush-lettered; when a number changes it is repainted rather than ticking digitally, with a quick fade between versions
Emphasis is a loose red circle or underline swash brushed around the key item, or two quick red slashes for a wrong answer
Charts are painted: bars or area fills as washes, axes as pencil lines, data points as small brushed dabs
Steps are separate vignettes painted along the sheet, linked by brushed arrows
sound: Soft wet brush touch-down followed by a hair-drag hiss matched to the stroke length
Low slow swells of water for washes flooding in, and occasional single soft drops
For scene changes, a brush swirled in a water pot, then knocked twice against its edge
A quiet room tone with a gentle warm pad; a bell-like chord on the key moment
avoid: Opaque flat fills, clean vector edges or solid black outlines
Gradients that look digital or perfectly even tints
Pure white painted on top; whites must come from unpainted paper
Fast snappy motion or hard cuts

name: Shadow Theatre
description: A live shadow play: flat black cut-out figures with lacy punched holes, pinned joints and thin sticks, pressed against a glowing cloth screen lit warm amber from behind, with coloured light showing through the holes.
suits: Good for stories, fables, history, cause-and-effect and anything told as a little performance; weak for precise numbers-heavy dashboards or bright modern tech topics.
look: The whole frame is a stretched cloth screen lit from behind by one lamp: brightest warm gold near the light source, sliding through orange to a deep reddish brown at the corners
All subjects are solid near-black silhouettes in strict profile, flat with no interior shading, as if cut from stiff hide or card
Silhouettes are decorated with punched cut-work: rows of small circles, teardrops, slits and lace-like patterns that let the screen light through
Some holes are backed with coloured gel, so they glow in jewel tones (teal, ruby, gold) instead of plain screen colour
Limbs and parts are separate pieces joined by visible round pin rivets, each a small punched ring around a dot
Thin dark control rods run from each figure down and out of the bottom edge, slightly blurred because they sit off the screen
Distance from the screen is shown by focus: pieces pressed flat are crisp, pieces held toward the lamp grow larger and very soft-edged
Text is cut out of hanging card plaques or banners on two strings, letters punched through so they glow; type is a classical serif
finish: Cloth weave multiplied over the frame: a fine regular grid of horizontal and vertical threads at low strength (around 6 to 8 percent darkening), plus large soft folds and slubs and one faint vertical seam
Light diffusion: a heavily blurred copy of the frame added back in screen mode at about 12 to 15 percent, so light bleeds into silhouette edges and halos the punched holes
Coarse grain refreshed at about 12 frames per second, low opacity
Dark warm vignette around the edges, fairly strong (about a third), and a slow gentle flicker of overall brightness from the flame
motion: Figures slide or hop in from the sides, carried by their sticks, with hinged parts swinging loosely on their pins and settling with a small pendulum wobble
Hanging plaques drop in on their strings, bounce and sway before coming to rest
The lamp is alive: overall light breathes and flickers subtly all the time, and flares on key moments

Scene changes use the theatre itself: a figure rushes toward the lamp until its blurred shape covers everything, the light dims to dark and comes back up, or two lacy drapes meet in the middle and draw apart
Pace is a storyteller's: deliberate movements with small character gestures, not snappy UI motion
explaining: Arrows are cut-paper vines or strips that grow along a curve, sprouting little leaves, ending in a spade-shaped head
Labels are small cut-letter plaques hung on a string from what they name
Numbers appear on a hanging board with punched-out digits that glow; counters swap digits with a small swing
Wrong or right is signalled by sliding a coloured gel over the lamp (red for wrong, warm gold for right) so the whole screen tints
Progress is shown as a physical climb or fill: a figure stepping up rungs, or a cut-out disc whose lit fraction grows
Emphasis is a burst of punched rays or sparks around the key item and a flare of the lamp
sound: Struck bronze tones, gamelan-like, with a slight beating detune, for things landing
Wooden clacks, ticks and ratchets for rods, joints and counters
A soft whump and sputter of an oil lamp catching, a low steady flame hum and occasional crackle
A deep gong for the key moment
avoid: Shading, gradients or colour inside the silhouettes other than gel-lit holes
Figures shown in three-quarter view or with visible faces drawn in detail
Clean white or cool backgrounds; the screen must always read as warm backlit cloth
Modern sans-serif UI text floating over the scene

name: Marker Whiteboard
description: A live whiteboard lesson: streaky dry-erase marker lines in black, blue, red and green drawn on a glossy white board, with wobbly boxes and arrows, faint smudges of earlier lessons and a soft overhead-light sheen.
suits: Good for processes, systems, business and teaching topics with a practical, classroom tone; less suited to emotional, cinematic or luxury subjects.
look: Surface is a bright cool white board with very faint large mottling from old cleaner, and gets slightly dimmer near its lower edge
Every line is a chisel-tip marker stroke: a slightly lighter wet middle, darker edges where ink gathers, ink density drifting along the stroke, and occasional dry streaks where the tip skipped
Ink pools into small darker blots where the marker lands and lifts
Shapes are drawn by hand: boxes and circles slightly wobbly, corners overshooting, important boxes traced twice so two lines nearly overlap
Colour has meaning: black for structure and text, blue for headings and main items, red for problems, loops and emphasis, green for results and right answers
Faint grey ghosts of previously erased diagrams sit under the live drawing, surviving in streaky bands where the eraser missed
Simple doodles stand in for objects: stick figures, cylinders, boxes, little icons, all in single-weight marker
Lettering is quick hand printing, letters jittered a little in size, angle and baseline
finish: Gloss pass over everything, ink included: two or three soft elongated white reflections of ceiling lights at low strength (around 15 to 25 percent), drifting slightly with camera moves
Ghost residue layer under the live ink: old marks at roughly 3 to 6 percent, broken up by a streaky eraser mask
Soft vertical darkening toward the lower part of the board, light (about 10 percent)
Optional aluminium frame and marker tray at the frame edge when the camera is wide
motion: Everything is drawn on live in sequence: each stroke grows from start to end at hand speed, with a short pen-lift pause between items
A marker held in a hand follows the current stroke tip, casting a soft shadow on the board
Text writes letter by letter; numbers are scribbled out and rewritten rather than morphing
The camera glides across one big board to reach new areas, with a slight breathing drift
Scene clearing is done with a felt eraser scrubbing back and forth, leaving ghost streaks behind
explaining: Arrows are single marker strokes with a slight curve and a quick two-stroke open head, sometimes traced twice for emphasis
Labels are written next to items, sometimes boxed or underlined twice
Key numbers are large hand-scrawled figures, circled in red or green when they land
Charts are hand-drawn axes with tick marks, bars hatched or filled with quick strokes, and a wobbly line for trends
Mistakes are crossed out with two hard red slashes; correct items get a green check
Cycles are drawn as a red looped arrow around a few boxed steps
sound: Felt-tip squeak and drag on a glossy surface, length matched to each stroke, with cap clicks between
A rapid scratchy scribble when writing numbers and words
Rough soft scrubbing of a felt eraser in rhythm with its passes
A low quiet room tone; a soft classroom bell-like tone on the key moment
avoid: Perfectly smooth vector lines or uniform stroke darkness
Filled gradients, shadows or 3D shading on drawings
Too many colours; stick to the four marker colours
Elements that fade or slide in instead of being drawn

name: Cosmic Swirl
description: A trippy night-sky poster: deep space filled with slowly churning liquid bands of loud complementary ink, star fields and glowing nebula, crossed by fine gold star-map linework, with fat swollen display lettering.
suits: Good for big-picture, mind-expanding, music, culture and 'how it all connects' topics with a playful or awe-struck tone; poor for sober, legal, medical or precise step-by-step instructions.
look: Base is a deep indigo-black night sky with a soft river of nebula glow running diagonally across it, cut by darker dust lanes
Over or inside the nebula run liquid concentric ring bands: stripes of flat saturated ink that warp and ripple like poured paint, each band edged by a thin dark key line
Colours come in clashing complementary pairs placed side by side (magenta against green, orange against blue, violet against yellow) so the edges seem to vibrate
Bands can be folded into a mirror-symmetric mandala around a centre point, like a kaleidoscope with 6 to 8 segments
Stars in three depths: tiny far dots, twinkling mid stars, and a few bright stars with a soft halo and four or six thin spikes
A star-map overlay in very fine gold and light cyan lines: dotted orbit ellipses with small open arrowheads, a graduated degree ring with tick marks, fine leader lines to small labels
Sunburst rays radiate from key objects, alternating long and short flame-like tongues
Big headings are bulbous, swollen display letters, gently warped column by column as if melting; small labels are elegant small-caps serif
finish: Misregistration: the dark outline layer sits slightly offset from the colour layer, about 1 to 2 pixels down and right, on all band and shape edges
Worn poster-stock pass: a warm cream fibre texture multiplied at low strength plus small cream speckles where ink has dropped out, cycling between three variants at about 8 frames per second
Soft additive glow on stars, nebula and the key object, with a gentle slow pulse
Fairly strong dark vignette (around a third to a half) so the edges sink into space
motion: The liquid bands churn constantly and slowly; their rings drift outward from the centre at a steady pace
Things arrive by blooming: colour ripples outward from a centre, petals or rays unfurl, stars fade up one by one
Headings melt or pour into place and then keep a slight wobble; chart lines engrave themselves on (rings sweep round, orbits dot on, labels land)
Scene changes are medium-native: a kaleidoscope spin into the next scene, a liquid melt pouring down, a ripple spreading from a point, or a short warp streak of stars
Pace builds: calm drift between beats, sudden intense colour on key moments
explaining: Arrows are dotted orbit arcs or striped ribbons of band colour that sweep from source to target, ending in a small open arrowhead
Labels are small-caps serif in gold, connected to their subject by a hairline leader, or set in cream chips outlined in dark ink
Key numbers are huge swollen display figures over a fine graduated scale, framed by a burst of rays when they land
Charts are star charts: data points are stars that appear one per step and join into a constellation, over a faint curved grid
Wrong is shown by colours clashing and jittering out of register and a red circle drawn round the target; right is the swirl folding into a calm symmetric mandala
Steps are stations on an orbit, each lighting up as a glowing marker travels round
sound: A slowly beating organ hum, swept by a phaser, over a low dark pad
Swirly phaser whooshes sweeping up and down for bands and transitions
Soft low radar-like pings for labels and stars landing, rising in pitch as a series builds
A big shimmering chord bloom with a low hit for the key moment; a sour detuned slide for wrong
avoid: Muted, pastel or tasteful colour; the ink pairs must be loud
Clean geometric sans-serif headings or crisp corporate UI elements
Photographic space imagery or realistic 3D rendering
Static frames; something must always be churning or twinkling

name: Neon Circuit
description: Slick tech motion graphics in a dark navy-to-violet void: glassy cards with hairline neon rims, line icons sitting in glowing tiles, and wired diagrams where bright sparks of light travel along the wires, with a soft bloom on everything bright.
suits: Strong for software, data, networks, AI and any system made of connected parts; too cold for warm human stories, nature, history or comedy.
look: Backdrop is a diagonal gradient from near-black navy to dark indigo, with four or five huge, very soft colour clouds (blue, violet, cyan, a touch of pink) that slowly wander and breathe in size.

The lower part of the frame is a floor grid seen in perspective: lines fan out from a vanishing point on the horizon and cross lines scroll steadily toward the viewer; the grid fades out near the horizon, which carries one thin bright haze line.
The upper part has a faint regular lattice of tiny dots that fades out toward the top, plus scattered drifting specks of light, a few with small halos, twinkling at different rates.

Content sits on dark see-through rounded cards: a big soft shadow below, two faint inner glows in accent colours at opposite corners, a hairline border that is bright cyan at one corner and fades toward the other, and a short white highlight along the top edge.
Icons are simple line drawings with round caps inside rounded-square tiles; the line itself is coloured with a cyan-to-violet gradient, and each tile floats in its own soft coloured halo.
Connections are smooth curves, thin and dim, with a short bright spark (white head, coloured tail) gliding along them; hubs are glowing points circled by thin rings.

Headlines are a bold geometric sans filled with one gradient running across the whole line, white into ice blue into violet; small capital eyebrow labels with wide letter spacing and a glowing dot in front.
Labels are capsule pills: dark fill, thin gradient outline, white medium-weight text, an optional coloured status dot on the left.
finish: Bloom on every frame, medium: copy the bright parts of the frame, blur them at a small and a wide radius, and add both back with additive blending so rims, icons, sparks and gradient type glow softly.
All halos, sparks, particles and flashes are drawn with additive blending, so overlaps brighten rather than cover.
A gentle dark vignette pulls the corners down, moderate strength.
No grain or noise of any kind: the surface stays clean and digital.
motion: Everything is eased: tiles and cards fade up while growing from a little under full size with a small overshoot; the line icon inside then traces itself on stroke by stroke.
Connections draw from source to target, then begin carrying sparks in a steady loop; when a spark arrives, the target flashes and a ring expands from it and fades.
Headlines build up word after word, each lifting from slightly below as it fades in.

One continuous virtual camera: a steady slow push-in through the whole piece, smooth pans to the next region while the backdrop moves slower than the content; a big change of idea is a fast dive through a hub with radial streaks of light and a brief white flash.
Things that stay relevant shrink and fly to a corner (a title becomes a small header) instead of vanishing.
Brisk, polished pace: entrances overlap, each a fraction of a second, with something new about every second.
explaining: Steps are a row of chips joined by wires; the active step brightens its rim and flashes its fill when a spark reaches it; a feedback loop is a curved return wire with a small arrowhead.
Right and wrong are colour signals: a mint spark and check badge for correct, a coral spark running backward along the wire for an error.
Key numbers are huge gradient numerals that count up quickly and slow as they settle, with a bloom flash on the final value; a small pill carries the unit.
Charts are line or area charts inside a card: a glowing gradient line, a filled area below that fades to transparent, a glowing point at the newest value, faint tick lines.
Emphasis is an expanding ring plus a brief extra glow on the element, never a shake.
The takeaway is a centred gradient headline with an underline that sweeps in from left to right.
sound: Soft, dull, filtered air whooshes for moves and camera pushes, kept low and gentle.
Short glassy blips when tiles land, and tiny digital ticks for counters that space out as the count settles.
A smooth rising sine glide while a spark travels a wire; a deep sub hit with a high shimmer on the key number.
A quiet sustained synth pad underneath that resolves to a bright major chord on the takeaway.
avoid: Light backgrounds, paper or grain textures, wobbly hand-drawn lines.
Pure primary red, green or yellow; glows stay in the cyan-blue-violet range, with coral and mint used only as signals.
Dropping the bloom pass or using hard shadows; without them it reads as a plain slide.
Clutter: one or two diagrams per frame with plenty of dark space around them.

name: Layered Paper
description: A shadow box of scissor-cut coloured card: every shape is its own sheet with a fibre texture, a slightly uneven cut edge and a soft shadow falling on the sheet behind, stacked in depth like the pages of an opened pop-up, under a warm lamp.
suits: Warm and friendly for stories, processes, places, growth and simple comparisons for a general audience; not right for dense numbers, fine detail or a cold high-tech tone.
look: The frame is built from stacked flat layers, back to front: a dark backboard, far shapes, middle shapes, a ground strip and a near foreground strip; each layer clearly floats above the one behind it.
Edges are cut, never drawn: straight edges wobble very slightly along their length, circles are slightly faceted polygons, curves are chains of short scissor snips; there are no outlines at all.

Each sheet is one flat matte colour overlaid with a tiling paper fibre texture (soft blotchy mottle, fine light and dark flecks, a few short hair-like fibres) at low contrast, placed at a different offset and angle on every sheet so it never repeats visibly.

Every sheet casts a two-part shadow onto the layer behind: a soft wide shadow offset down and to the right (wider for sheets that sit higher) and a thin dark contact line hugging the edge; the top-left cut edge catches a one-pixel light rim and the bottom-right edge a one-pixel dark rim.
Torn edges (hilltops, ground, banners) are ragged and reveal a thin band of white fibrous paper core, with tiny fibres poking out, between the coloured face and whatever lies behind.
Detail is added by gluing on smaller pieces or punching holes: windows punched out to show the layer behind, small punched stars, grass made of little upward snips cut into a green strip.
Headlines are a chunky heavy sans cut from coloured paper and mounted on a cream backing sheet trimmed loosely around the whole word with a margin; each letter tilts a degree or two.
Small labels are folded paper tags or little standing card tents with a visible crease, propped against what they name; a fine dotted fold line can mark where a card bends.
finish: Warm desk-lamp light from the top left on every frame: a soft-light radial pass that is creamy warm near the lamp and cools to a dim blue-purple in the far corners, moderate strength; optionally a second, fainter warm pool over the area being explained.
A plum-tinted vignette, medium strength.
Very light film grain, refreshed about twelve times a second so it shimmers like a photographed set.
motion: Pieces enter three ways: rise from below the way a pop-up page stands when opened; drop in from above with a little overshoot, the shadow wide and soft while airborne and tightening as it lands; or spring out from a point.
The camera pans sideways along one long diorama; far layers move much less than near ones, giving strong parallax depth, and a slow push-in settles each station.
Small idle loops keep it alive: pieces flutter by swapping between two or three cut versions of their shape, hanging items sway on a thin wire.
Exits: pieces sink back down behind the ground strip or lift off upward; a real change of scene is a long pan to the next station of the diorama.
Moderate, tactile pace; groups and words fall on as a staggered ripple a few hundredths of a second apart.
explaining: Arrows are thick paper strips with a cut triangular head that grow along a gentle curve, each with its own shadow.
Numbers are separate cut-out digit tiles, each a little rotated; when a value changes, tiles are flicked out and swapped rather than smoothly counted.
Bar charts are paper strips that climb into view from below the ground strip, with a thin paper strip for the axis and folded tags for values.
To stress the key item, a ring of card or a fan of cut rays pops up behind it, plus a slight push-in.
Right and wrong are a cut green tick or a cut red cross dropped onto the item; a speech bubble is a cut card that flips over to show its other side.
sound: A light card tap (soft thump plus a small paper snap) for every piece that lands.
A big, low, smooth rub of cardstock sliding past cardstock for camera pans, with no crinkle.
A dry short slide ending in a tap for strips pushing out, quick flicks for digit tiles, a springy pop-up page sound for the emphasis burst.
Quiet room tone; optional soft plucked music low in the mix.
avoid: Outlines, gradients inside a shape, glossy highlights or perfectly smooth vector curves.
Sheets without shadows or all layers at one depth; that flattens it into clip art.
Many tiny fiddly pieces; shapes should be big and simple, as if cut by hand with scissors.

name: Clay Stop-Motion
description: Plasticine stop-motion on a small sculpted set: chunky hand-pressed shapes with soft waxy shading, fingerprints and tool smears, lumpy edges, animated in held poses with a gentle surface boil.
suits: Playful, friendly topics: learning for kids, everyday habits, simple cause and effect, product stories with charm; poor for precise data, dense text or serious and technical subjects.
look: Every object is a thick rounded lump: a simple silhouette with soft irregular bulges, corners always rounded, and it looks inflated, highest in the middle and rolling off toward the edge.

Shading comes from that implied height: a warm key light from the top left, broad soft falloff, a small dull sheen on the top (waxy, not glossy), and the shadow side slightly warmer and richer in colour, as if light glows through the clay.
The surface shows the maker's hands: a few partial fingerprints (fine curved ridges fading at the edges), shallow tool grooves with a slightly raised lip, and faint broad lumpiness.

The set is a back wall of smeared clay, slightly out of focus and lit by a warm pool of light, above a clay tabletop slab whose front edge curves down and darkens; a few stray crumbs of clay lie about.
Objects sitting on the table get a soft dark contact patch beneath them, plus a soft drop shadow down and to the right.
Letters and digits are separate rolled-clay glyphs in a rounded bold face, each its own lump, often each a different colour, slightly rotated, standing proud of the surface.
Colours are saturated toy primaries softened toward warm; any eyes are white balls with glossy black pupils.
finish: Warm colour grade on every frame: a soft-light pass from peach in the top left to cool blue-grey in the bottom right, moderate.
Exposure flicker that changes on every held pose, a small random lift or dip in brightness, as with real stop-motion frames.
A warm dark-brown vignette, medium strength, and softly blurred far edges of the set for shallow depth of field.
Fine grain, light, re-seeded on each held pose.
motion: Everything moves on twos: each pose is held for two frames of a 24 fps rhythm, with no smooth in-between motion.
Boil: the fine surface noise and fingerprint ridges shift slightly on every new pose, so even still objects look freshly touched.
Entrances pop on in a few discrete poses: squashed flat and wide, stretched tall, a small overshoot, then settled.
Exits are physical: knocked off so they fall with gravity and tumble out the bottom of the frame, or shoved off to the side, speeding up as they go.
Moves along the table are slides in visible steps; a word appears letter by letter, one new letter per pose.
explaining: Arrows are rolled snakes of clay with a pinched point, laid down along their path.
Numbers are pressed clay digits; when a value changes, the digits are replaced by freshly sculpted ones with a small pop, never a smooth count.
Charts are clay bars that push up through the tabletop: each starts squashed flat and stretches up to its height.
Wrong is a red clay cross pushed onto the item with a short shake; right is a green clay tick; the key moment gets a gold clay star or the item swelling and changing colour.
Labels are clay letters pressed into a flat slab of clay; keep words short and big.
sound: A soft low wet plop for each piece popping on, one per pose in which new letters appear.
Squelches for squash and stretch, a dull slap when a coil is laid down.
Dull thuds offscreen for knocked-off pieces, a smeary slide for shoves.
Optional light plucky toy music, very low.
avoid: Sharp corners, thin lines, perfect geometry, or smooth tweened motion at full frame rate.
Glossy plastic highlights or flat unshaded fills; it must read as matte waxy clay.
Long sentences or small text.

name: X-Ray Lightbox
description: X-ray films clipped to a glowing viewing box in a dark reading room: subjects show as translucent white density on blue-black film, marked up with grease pencil, masking tape and typed ID labels.
suits: Ideal for look-inside explanations: anatomy, how a mechanism works, hidden structure, faults and diagnosis, before and after inspections; poor for colourful, playful or emotional topics.
look: The viewing box is an evenly lit cool-white panel with a few soft brighter zones where the tubes sit behind the diffuser, faint banding and a gentle fall-off toward its edges; the room around it is almost black.

Film is a negative: where nothing blocks the rays it is deep blue-black; density adds up, so thicker or harder parts are brighter and overlapping parts brighter still; soft tissue-like parts are a faint grey haze around crisp white hard structures.
Subjects are built from additive translucent layers: hollow parts show as bright rims around darker centres, like tubes seen from the side; any metal comes out almost pure white with sharp edges.
Each film has a lighter grey-blue unexposed border around the exposed rectangle, with crisp edges; whole films hang very slightly rotated.

Small blocky lead-letter markers glow bright white inside the field near a corner; an ID patch (a pale rectangle with dark typewriter text) sits in another corner; tiny edge printing runs along the margin.
Films hang from chrome spring clips along their top edge (small metallic blocks with a dark pivot).
Annotations are grease pencil in waxy yellow, red and green, drawn as broken, slightly doubled strokes; headers are on strips of masking tape with zigzag torn ends.
finish: Halation on every frame: a wide soft glow spreading from the brightest dense parts onto the film around them, low strength.
Film mottle and grain: broad uneven blotches plus fine per-pixel grain, stronger in the thin areas, re-seeded every frame.
Per-film wear that travels with the film: a few faint bright near-vertical scratches, scattered dark dust specks, a handful of bright pinholes.
Lightbox bleed: bright glass around the film edges glows outward over them (screen-blended blur, medium), plus a slight dark vignette.
motion: Opening: the box's tubes flicker on one at a time, stuttering before they hold steady, and the room brightens with them.
A fresh film develops: it starts as milky grey fog, then the dark base and bright density arrive as a front sweeping from top to bottom with a ragged, mottled edge.
Scene change: the current film is tugged free of its clips and drops away; the next is slapped up from above and settles with a small bounce and flex.
Grease pencil writes at hand speed, revealed along the stroke; text appears left to right as if being written.
A slow, steady push-in on the box across the whole piece.
explaining: Arrows, rings and notes are drawn in wax pencil straight onto the glass: rings are loose ovals that overshoot where they started; arrows are curved strokes finished with two quick head strokes.
Counters are typed in the ID patch in monospace, changing in place.
Updated values are handwritten: the old value is struck through with one line and the new one written beside it.
Headers and the takeaway are bold marker capitals on masking tape stuck across the top or bottom of the box.
Wrong gets a red pencil ring and slash; right gets a green tick; the key number gets two quick red rings.
sound: Fluorescent tubes tinking and buzzing on, then a low ballast hum under everything.
A waxy grease-pencil drag in short grains, lasting exactly as long as each stroke draws.
Metallic spring-clip snaps and the low wobbly flex of a film sheet when films are pulled or slapped up; a tape tear and press.
A knuckle knock on the glass for the wrong moment and the key number; a dry mechanical clack for each ID counter change.
avoid: Positive images (dark subject on light film), coloured fills inside the film, solid opaque shapes with no translucency.
Clean vector text on the film; every word is typed ID, grease pencil, or marker on tape.
A bright room or a warm palette; the only light comes from the box.

name: Cute Sticker
description: Flat pastel kawaii illustration: chunky rounded shapes with soft plum outlines and a single cel shade, glossy big-eyed faces, sparkles and hearts over a polka-dot backdrop, with key pieces finished like die-cut stickers.
suits: Light, friendly topics: kids, onboarding, wellness, consumer apps, simple how-tos; poor for serious, sad, or data-heavy technical subjects.
look: Shapes are chunky and rounded: circles, capsules and rectangles with big corner radii; nothing has a sharp corner.
One outline colour for everything, a deep soft plum, medium-thick and even, with round joins; the overlapping parts of one object share a single outer outline so no inner seams show.

Fills are flat pastels with exactly one cel-shade tone: the whole shape is filled in the deeper shade, then the base colour is drawn shifted up and left inside it, leaving a crescent of shade at the bottom right; one small white highlight oval near the top left.
Faces, when used, have big glossy eyes (dark upper lid, iris shading from dark to light, large pupil, two white catchlight dots), pink blush ovals and a tiny mouth.
Backdrops are one flat pastel colour with a slowly drifting staggered pattern of small dots, stars or hearts in a slightly deeper tint, plus big soft white clouds with no outline.
Key items get the sticker treatment: a thick white border around the plum outline and a small soft shadow, as if die-cut and stuck on.
Lettering is a very rounded bold face with white fill, a thick pink or plum outline and a soft shadow below; letters may cycle through the pastels.
Decorations: four-point twinkles, little hearts, short motion lines, and comic emote marks.
finish: No grain, no texture: colours stay clean and flat on every frame.
Soft plum shadows at low opacity under lettering and stickers only, never under background shapes.
Twinkles blink on and off in empty areas of the frame, away from content.
motion: Animated on twos, so motion has a light hand-drawn stepping.
Bouncy pop for every entrance: grows from nothing, overshoots past full size and settles with a damped wobble, alternating squash and stretch.
Letters pop on one at a time, each with a little hop off the baseline.
Idle life: things bob gently up and down and wiggle; every landing squashes.
Scene changes are iris wipes shaped like a star or a heart, growing from a point and framed by a fat candy-coloured border (plum outside, pink or butter inside, a thin white line).
explaining: Connectors are rows of round candy dots appearing one after another along a curve, finished with a chunky rounded triangle arrowhead.
Numbers are big outlined bubbly numerals that give a little bounce every time they change.
Charts are rounded bars popping up one after another; a small marker can hop from bar to bar.

Emotion carries emphasis: a wrong answer earns a big rounded X stamp, spiral eyes, a sweat bead and a ?!; a right answer earns sparkle eyes, floating hearts and confetti; the key moment gets a quick punch-in with a tiny shake.
Labels are rounded sticker pills or speech bubbles with the plum outline.
sound: Soft boings and bubbly pops for each entrance, kept low-mid and never harsh.
Twinkly chimes for sparkles, a quick rising arpeggio for right, a soft falling slide for wrong.
A squeaky-toy squeeze or light thump for stamps; an optional light bouncy music bed, very low.
avoid: Black or heavy dark outlines, realistic shading, gradients or textures.
Sharp angular shapes and loud saturated colours.
Dense text; keep words short and large.

name: Field Guide Plate
description: An old natural-history book plate on aged cream paper inside a pressed border: specimens drawn in fine brown-black engraved line, washed with thin watercolour that strays slightly off the lines, each tagged with a figure number and an italic caption.
suits: Good for calm, careful explanations of parts, kinds, stages and anatomy (biology, how a thing is built, classification); poor for fast, loud, hype or very digital topics.
look: Every form is shaded with engraved lines: parallel strokes that follow the curve of the surface, swelling thicker in shadow and thinning to a hair at both ends.
Outlines are heavier on the side away from the light (light from upper left) and fine on the lit side.
The darkest shadows get a second set of lines crossing the first at a shallow angle; small round parts are shaded with fine stipple dots instead.
Colour is a separate thin wash under the ink: soft and uneven, a little off the lines, with a darker rim where the pigment dried at its edge and a mottled, granular density inside.
Subjects are isolated specimens on bare paper with plenty of space around them, each with a small italic figure number (Fig. 1, Fig. 2) close by, laid out like a scientific plate.
A thin double ruled frame sits inside a slightly darker pressed rectangle; tiny running heads in the top corners (volume, plate number) and a centred italic caption line at the bottom.
Paper is warm cream, browner toward the edges, with scattered rust-brown foxing spots gathered mostly near the margins.
Lettering is a classic old-style serif: widely letter-spaced roman capitals for headings, italic for names and captions.
finish: Tint layer multiplied under the ink, nudged a pixel or two off register and softened slightly; medium strength, the colour must look added by hand after printing.
Ink is never pure black: a warm brown-black with a faint soft halo, as if the lines sank a little into damp paper; subtle.
Paper grain, foxing spots and a darkening toward the sheet edges; gentle, aged but never dirty.
A debossed border: a thin dark line with a pale highlight just outside it; light.
Fine grain over the whole frame, re-seeded several times a second; very light.
motion: Ink line comes first; shortly after, the colour spreads outward from the middle of each figure with a ragged wet edge.
New lines engrave themselves along their length, start to finish, as if cut by a tool; hatching fills in stroke by stroke.
Specimens may sway or flex very slightly (a stem, a feeler, a hinge); nothing bounces or squashes.
To move to a new scene, a fresh plate comes off the press: a soft vertical shadow band sweeps left to right and the new plate is revealed behind it.
Pace is unhurried; holds are long, and any camera move is a slow drift or gentle push-in.
explaining: Labels are small italic captions linked to their subject by a fine engraved leader line ending in a dot.
Arrows are engraved: a tapering shaft, a narrow barbed head and a feathered tail, drawn on from tail to head.
Numbers sit inside an engraved cartouche (an ornamented oval or scroll with a ruled edge); values roll over in serif numerals.
Steps or stages are numbered figures in a row or around a circle, joined by engraved arrows, like a life-cycle plate.
Emphasis is the colourist's brush: a loose red watercolour ring around the key figure, or a red wash cross through a wrong one; a green ring for correct.
Charts become growth series: the same specimen drawn at several sizes side by side, each labelled with its stage or value.
sound: Dry, gritty scratch of a metal tool cutting copper while lines draw on.
Heavy rolling drum and a damp paper peel for each new plate.
Soft wet brush swish when a wash or ring is painted.
Small brass clicks or a numbering-wheel tick for counters, over a quiet warm pad.
avoid: Flat vector fills, solid black masses or uniform line weight.
Saturated or neon colour, smooth gradients, glows or drop shadows.
Modern sans-serif type or rounded UI boxes.
Fast bouncy motion or cartoon squash and stretch.

name: Linocut Print
description: A bold black and vermilion relief print on off-white paper, with a pencilled title and edition number below: the image is white carved out of solid black with pointed knife cuts, and the ink sits patchy and speckled.
suits: Good for bold, folk, craft or activist tones, simple processes and one strong idea per beat; poor for fine detail, dense data or many small labels.
look: Think in reverse: the block starts solid black and the image is what gets cut away. White marks are pointed cuts, fat in the middle and sharp at both ends, or teardrop cuts that start wide and taper to a point.
Tone comes from rows of parallel cuts: close cuts read light, sparse cuts read dark; the cuts follow the contour of whatever they shade (hills, bodies, rings).
Around carved shapes and just inside the block border sit short stray nicks and chips, as if the cutter's hand slipped; open black is never perfectly clean.
The block is a rectangle with a softly wavy edge and a thin cut line just inside it, printed with a wide paper margin all round.
The second colour is a vermilion red printed from its own block: usually one large shape behind the black (a disc, a band, a fill) plus a few accents.
Lettering looks hand cut: heavy block capitals, each letter slightly rotated and nudged up or down; often paper-coloured letters cut out of a red or black band.
In the margin under the block, pencil writing: a title at the left, an edition number such as 3/20 and a signature at the right.
finish: Ragged ink edges: block shapes softened a hair, then cut off against a noise threshold so every edge is slightly rough; medium.
Speckle: small patches where paper shows through dense black and red, as if the ink skipped the high points of the sheet; clearly visible, but black still reads as solid.
Red printed a few pixels out of register with the black, so a sliver of red peeks out along one side of shapes; light to medium.
Paper: warm off-white with long thin pale and tan fibres, a faint pressed outline around the block and a soft warm vignette; light.
Pencil marks are grey and grainy and skip across the paper tooth; light.
motion: The print updates in stop-motion steps, about eight a second, as if each frame were a new pull; nothing glides smoothly inside the block.
Opening: the sheet lifts off the inked block along a diagonal front, red appearing first and black after, with a thin soft shadow just ahead of the lifting edge.
Scene changes are new proofs: the next print is peeled in over the old one along the same diagonal sweep.
New shapes appear as if being carved: cuts draw on one stroke at a time and lines grow along their length.
After a print lands, a faint raking sheen of wet ink slides once across the black; then it holds. The camera at most eases in slowly.
explaining: Arrows are white channels gouged through the black, tapering, with a triangular head; when something goes wrong, the path prints in red instead.
Numbers are big chunky cut numerals, re-cut on every step so they flicker slightly as they change.
Labels are paper-coloured letters cut from a red band, or black letters on a cleared patch; few words, set large.
Emphasis is done by hand in pencil: a loose ring around the key thing, plus a few scribbled words under the block.
Charts are carved bars or a filled area: red fill under a black outline, with cut hatching over it.
Separate items or steps are small carved tiles in a row, each a paper square holding a black-line picture.
sound: Crunchy scrape of a V-shaped cutter through lino while cuts and arrows draw on.
Tacky crackle and a paper lift when a proof is peeled.
A heavy press coming down with a deep wooden knock for the big moment.
Pencil scratching for notes and signature; small dry knocks for numerals.
avoid: Smooth anti-aliased vector shapes, gradients or soft shading.
More than two ink colours, any glow, or transparency.
Hairlines or even-width outlines; every mark is a tapering cut.
Fluid tweening inside the print.

name: Voxel Blocks
description: A cheerful toy world built from coloured cubes on a warm peach backdrop, seen from above at a fixed three-quarter angle, with soft shadows and darkened creases where blocks meet, and each cube's top brighter than its two sides.
suits: Good for playful, friendly explanations of systems, places, building up and step-by-step assembly; poor for serious, abstract, emotional or text-heavy topics.
look: Everything is unit cubes on a grid in an orthographic three-quarter view: top face lightest, the face toward camera a mid tone, the far side darkest, with a slightly cool tint on the sides and warm on top.
Each visible face darkens softly toward edges and corners that touch other cubes, so inside corners and stair steps pick up gentle dark creases.
Light comes from high at the back left; faces that something blocks from that light are darker and lean slightly purple.
Scenes stand on a thick base slab with a grass or tile top and a stepped brown underside that gets darker the deeper it goes, floating above a big blurred shadow on the backdrop.
Within one material each cube's colour varies a little, so surfaces look hand-placed rather than flat.
Bright parts (lights, screens, indicators) are glowing cubes: flat, near-white-tinted colour with a soft halo around them.
Background is a smooth warm peach studio sweep, lighter toward the middle.
Text is either chunky pixel lettering built from extruded cubes, or flat floating tags: cream rectangles with a darker extruded side and bottom edge and a soft drop shadow.
finish: Soft crease darkening on every face that touches neighbours, every frame; medium, it is what sells the look.
Cast shadows inside the scene and a blurred contact shadow under the floating base; medium.
Additive glow halos around glowing cubes; light.
Warm edge vignette and a very fine static grain; very light.
motion: Builds: cubes drop in from above and land with a small ease-out, course by course, starting at the bottom, each one slightly offset in time so it reads as a shower.
Movement happens in whole-cube steps (things on a belt hop one cube at a time); characters or parts may bob gently.
The camera turns a few degrees while something builds, then trucks sideways along one long scene to reach the next area instead of cutting.
Tags and labels pop in with a small overshoot and shrink away to leave.
Pace is cheerful and steady, a new beat every second or two.
explaining: Arrows are a dotted trail of small cubes along a gentle arc, appearing one cube at a time; a red trail for an error travelling back.
Pictures, icons, ticks and crosses are tiny pixel art made of cubes standing upright.
Numbers sit on floating tags in pixel lettering and tick upward; the key number swells big and throws out a ring of little square blocks.
Charts are columns of stacked cubes, one per step, rising block by block with their value tag riding on top.
Emphasis: blocky corner brackets snap in around the thing and blink a couple of times.
sound: Hollow plastic click as each block snaps into place; a light patter of tiny clicks while a build rains down.
A bigger thunk when a stack lands together.
Short bright toy chimes for correct, a dull boop for wrong.
avoid: Perspective distortion, curved surfaces or any non-cube shape in the world.
Black outlines or flat cartoon shading without the three face tones.
Dark, cold or gritty palettes.
Text painted flat onto the world without a tag or extrusion.

name: Halftone Comic
description: A vintage comic page blown up big and framed as a strip of panels on yellowed newsprint: flat yellow and primary colours, red and blue printed dot fields, heavy brush-inked black outlines, and comic captions, balloons and bursts, slightly off register.
suits: Good for punchy, dramatic, fun or myth-busting topics with clear turns and surprises; poor for quiet, nuanced or data-dense subjects.
look: Shapes are flat fills outlined in heavy black ink that swells and tapers like a brush, sometimes with a second, slightly offset outline as if inked twice.
Mid tones are dot fields: round dots of one colour on a staggered grid (every other row shifted half a step); dot size can grow toward one side to suggest shading.
Colour is limited to flat bright yellow, red, blue, black and paper white; red dots for warm skin-like tones, blue dots for sky, shade and backgrounds.
Shine and form are drawn as solid black shapes and sharp white streaks, never gradients.
Panels have thick black borders on a white page with gutters between them; the whole story is one long strip.
Comic devices: a yellow caption box in a panel corner, white oval speech balloons with a pointed tail, bubble-trail thought balloons, jagged explosion bursts, short motion and shock lines.
Lettering is all-caps comic hand lettering in black, tilted a little for impact, with key words bigger; letters sit on a white knockout outline that breaks the dots behind them.
finish: Two plates: all colour (fills and dots) on one layer, black line on another; the colour layer shifted a few pixels off register, then the black multiplied over it; clearly visible at edges.
Newsprint ageing: paper a touch yellower and darker toward the frame edges, with a faint broad blotchy tone and fine fibre noise; light.
Each dot wobbles a hair in size and position so the screen looks printed, not computed; subtle.
motion: Things spring in with a fast overshoot (a quick swell, then settle), never a slow fade.
Dot fields arrive as a wave sweeping across the area, dots popping on in order.
Balloon and caption text slams in one word at a time.
Between beats the view glides along the strip to the next panel; mid-glide it widens slightly so neighbouring panels and white gutters show, then tightens again.
Big moments get a short shake and a slow push-in.
explaining: Arrows are thick curved arrows filled yellow with a heavy black outline, drawn on from tail to head.
Numbers burst out of jagged explosion balloons in huge lettering; counters flip quickly.
Labels go in caption boxes or balloons pointing at the thing; sound-effect words (POW, ZIP) mark actions.
Emphasis: a red and yellow burst holding a one-word verdict plus a screen shake; a ray sunburst behind a winner.
Charts are simple bars outlined in black and filled with flat colour or dots, springing up one by one on a framed board.
sound: Short punchy thwack when lettering lands.
A thud plus a crash of noise for explosion bursts.
Quick low zip for arrows and objects whipping on; a soft smooth slide when the view glides across the page.
Tiny dry clicks for counters.
avoid: Gradients, soft shadows or blur.
Thin even vector strokes or modern UI type.
Muted, pastel or many-colour palettes.
Clean, perfectly registered digital colour without dot texture.

name: Pixel Arcade
description: A 16-bit console game scene with blue menu windows and typed text over scenery in stacked layers: chunky pixels enlarged with hard edges, a small fixed palette, and dithered stripes where colours meet.
suits: Good for playful, game-like or step-by-step explanations of progress, levels, trial and error; poor for photoreal, delicate or very formal topics.
look: Draw everything on a small pixel buffer (about 256 by 144) and enlarge it five times with smoothing off; every edge is a hard stair step and nothing sits between pixels.
Use a fixed palette of a few dozen colours grouped in ramps (each material gets 3 to 5 shades from dark to light); no colour outside it.
Smooth blends are faked: skies are horizontal stripes of flat colour with a thin seam of ordered (Bayer) dither between neighbours; glows and haze dither too.
Depth comes from layers that scroll at different speeds: far hills or skyline in muted cool colours with a lit rim facing the light, nearer layers darker and richer.
Sprites are small, with a dark one-pixel outline and a lighter rim on the lit side; stars, windows and sparks are single pixels.
Menus and dialogs are windows with a dark outer edge, a white border, a grey inner line and a deep blue top-to-bottom gradient fill (dithered), corners slightly clipped.
Text is a crisp pixel font with a one-pixel dark drop shadow: gold for names and headers, white for body.
finish: Hard-pixel upscale with smoothing off, every frame; full strength, it is the medium.
Palette lock: every drawn colour comes from the fixed palette, and blends happen only through dither; full strength.
Positions snap to whole low-res pixels and logic advances on a coarse game tick (about ten steps a second), so motion is a little steppy; full.
Fades go through a handful of discrete brightness levels, never a smooth fade.
motion: Openings: brightness steps up from black and scenery layers climb up from below one pixel at a time, far layers first.
Characters walk with a two-frame cycle and bob by one pixel; small items blink.
Windows snap open by growing in a few steps, then text types out letter by letter, with a bouncing next-arrow once it is done.
Scene changes use console transitions: the image breaks into big blocks and resolves again, a wavy sideways ripple, or a circle that closes to black and reopens on the next scene.
Hits get a one-frame bright flash and a short shake.
explaining: The headline lives in a small menu window in a top corner, like a quest title.
Labels and numbers sit in windows; counters tick up like a score with leading zeros; stats are segmented bars that fill in steps.
Arrows are pixel chevrons or a line of marching dots; error paths are red dotted trails.
Choices or steps are a command menu with a small pointing-hand or triangle cursor that jumps between options.
Emphasis: big outlined pop-up words (HIT!, MISS!) that rise and fade, sparkles, a level-up style banner.
Charts are stepped bars or an experience bar filling left to right.
sound: Square and pulse wave blips for typed text and cursor moves.
A noise burst with a pitch sweep for transitions.
A short rising arpeggio for success, a low buzz for a miss.
A simple looping chiptune bed under each scene.
avoid: Smooth scaling, anti-aliased edges, sub-pixel motion or blur.
Colours outside the palette or smooth gradients.
High-resolution vector type laid over the pixel art.
Scanline or CRT filters; keep it clean console pixels.

name: Retro Paint Desktop
description: A chunky-pixel 1990s computer screen: teal wallpaper, grey bevelled windows with navy title bars, and a bitmap paint program where someone doodles the explanation live with crude mouse strokes, bucket fills and typed text boxes.
suits: Good for playful, nostalgic walk-throughs of software, computing ideas, step-by-step procedures and everyday tech; a poor fit for solemn subjects, luxury tones or charts that need fine precision.
look: The whole screen is drawn at half resolution and then doubled, so every edge is a hard square pixel step and nothing is smoothed.

Desktop: a flat teal wallpaper with a few 32-pixel icons (white caption under each, caption turns navy-highlighted when picked) and a grey taskbar along the bottom with a launcher button at the left, task buttons in the middle and a sunken clock tray at the right.

Windows are light grey slabs with a two-pixel bevel (white and pale grey on the top and left edges, dark grey and black on the bottom and right), a solid navy title strip with a bold white bitmap caption, and three small square caption buttons at the right end.

The main window is a bitmap paint program: a menu row with one underlined letter per word, a two-column toolbox of square tool buttons (the active one pressed in and filled with a one-pixel checker), a sunken white canvas with a stippled scrollbar, a two-row strip of colour swatches and a status bar showing the pointer's x,y position.

Marks on the canvas look made by an unsteady hand with a mouse: 1 to 3 pixel aliased strokes that wobble a little and sometimes overshoot their corners, rectangles and ellipses from the shape tools with slightly unequal sides, and stroke ends that do not quite meet.

Bucket fills are perfectly flat colour that floods to the nearest closed edge, and they leak out through any gap left in an outline; airbrush marks are a loose cloud of single scattered pixels, denser in the middle.
Text is either the tiny bitmap system face in the window chrome, or larger hand-style lettering typed into the canvas with the text tool, always hard-edged and often sitting on an opaque colour box.

Dialog boxes are small grey windows with a pixel icon (red circle with white cross for errors, blue speech balloon with an i for information), one or two lines of message and a grey push button whose default state has a black outer ring and a dotted inner focus line.
The mouse pointer is always on screen and changes with the job: black-edged white arrow, thin crosshair for drawing tools, I-beam for typing, hourglass while busy.
finish: Pixel doubling at full strength: render to a half-size buffer and scale up with nearest-neighbour on every frame; all positions and sizes snap to whole buffer pixels.
Hard text threshold at full strength: every glyph pixel is fully on or fully off, so even the large hand lettering has jagged stair-step curves.
Ordered two-by-two dither instead of any tonal blend: used sparingly, only for pressed buttons, the scrollbar track, an active task button and any colour band that needs a transition.
Pointer drawn last on every frame, above everything, so the screen always feels operated by a person.
motion: Strokes replay at real mouse-drag speed with the pointer riding the tip; the line grows behind it in pixel steps, and shape tools stretch from one corner to the opposite corner.
Bucket fills appear whole in a single frame with no easing; airbrush speckle builds up over a fraction of a second while the button is held; the text caret blinks about twice a second.
Windows open with two or three thin grey outline rectangles racing from the source (an icon or task button) to the final frame, then the full window appears at once; closing runs it in reverse.
Scene changes are the screen's own: the canvas scrolls sideways with the scrollbar thumb sliding, a property-sheet tab is clicked by the pointer, or a window closes and another zooms open.
Progress bars fill in separate solid blocks; a frozen dialog dragged across the screen leaves a staircase of stale copies behind it until something repaints.
Pace is brisk and literal: things pop or snap rather than glide, one change every one to two seconds, with the pointer travelling between jobs in short purposeful moves.
explaining: Labels are typed into a dashed text box one key at a time, with the I-beam caret blinking at the end; a retyped number is erased with a white box and typed again.
Arrows are line-tool strokes in black or red with a crude two-stroke V head, or chains of 2-pixel dots with a solid pixel triangle at the end when they live in the window chrome.
Emphasis: a thick red brush cross slashed over a wrong answer, a red ellipse-tool ring round the key item, and a green hand-drawn tick for the right one.

Quantities sit in the interface: counters in sunken fields or the status bar, adjustable amounts as horizontal trackbar sliders with tick marks, related items gathered inside etched group boxes with a caption breaking the top edge.
Charts are drawn by hand on the canvas: pencil axes, a stepped climbing line, bars filled with the bucket; copies of an example pile up as repeated pasted stamps, each slightly offset.
The takeaway lands as a small message box with an icon, one sentence and an OK button that the pointer clicks.
sound: Plastic mouse-button clicks, a sharp press and a lighter release, bracketing every drag, with a soft rubbing of the mouse across the desk mat during each stroke.
Keyboard key taps for each typed character, thinned so fast typing never becomes a buzz; scroll-wheel clicks as the canvas pans.
A short rising 'bloop' for each bucket fill, a soft hiss for the airbrush, hard-disk head chatter while things copy, and a made-up two-note chime for dialogs with a dull low thunk for errors.
A very quiet computer fan and mains hum underneath everything.
avoid: Any anti-aliasing, soft shadows, rounded corners, translucency or smooth gradients; these instantly make it look modern.
Real product names, logos, flag emblems or recognisable trademark app icons; keep every caption and icon generic.
Smooth eased motion or motion blur; this medium snaps and pops.
Neat, perfect vector drawing on the canvas; the charm is that it is clearly painted by hand with a mouse.

name: Bauhaus Geometry
description: A modernist workshop print from the 1920s: flat red, yellow, blue and black geometric shapes and bar-built lettering on a strict grid, printed on worn cream poster paper with slightly offset colour plates.
suits: Strong for systems, structures, processes and design or engineering ideas told with clarity and confidence; weak for soft emotional stories, organic nature subjects or anything that needs photographic realism.
look: Ground is a warm cream poster sheet that darkens toward tan at the edges, with faint paper fibre streaks and a scatter of small soft brown age spots.
Layout sits on a visible modular grid of thin black rules, laid out asymmetrically with generous empty cream, and often one long diagonal construction rule cutting behind the main figure.
Every figure is assembled from nothing but circles, squares, half-discs, triangles and straight bars in flat solid colour; shapes have no outlines and simply touch or overlap.
A very large disc usually sits behind the main subject like a sun or halo, and smaller primitives are stacked on top to make faces, machines or objects.
Display lettering is lower-case and constructed from the same parts: vertical bars for stems, full rings for bowls, partial arcs for shoulders, all of one stroke weight.
Running text, tags and numbers use a clean geometric grotesque in bold; reversed words are knocked out to bare paper inside solid colour blocks.
A short label is often turned 90 degrees and set along a vertical rule at the side of the sheet.
finish: Colour separation offset, medium: each of the four inks is drawn on its own layer, where a shape in one colour also punches a matching hole in the other three, then the layers are printed with small different nudges (one or two pixels each way) so thin overlap slivers darken and thin paper gaps show.
Ink mottle, medium-light: ink coverage drops in soft cloudy patches by up to about a fifth, with rare tiny pinholes where paper shows through solid areas.
Fold creases, light: one vertical and one horizontal crease cross the sheet, each a narrow pale-then-dark band with small paper scuffs along it.
Grain and edge darkening, light: fine moving grain at a few percent and a gentle warm brown vignette.
motion: The grid rules draw out first, then shapes drop onto the sheet and settle with a small overshoot, like wooden blocks set down on a table.
Details stamp on one at a time in quick succession; the bar-built letters are placed individually, each dropping to the baseline.
The story lives on one long wide sheet; between beats the camera tracks sideways along it to the next panel and comes to a firm stop.
At the end the camera pulls out until the entire sheet reads as a single diagram.
During holds only small mechanical movements continue: a dial ratchets round in steps, arcs pulse outward, a token keeps circling a loop.
explaining: Arrows are a thick black bar ending in a large solid triangle, drawn by the bar extending from its start.
Labels are solid black rectangles with bold cream text that drop onto whatever they name with a small bounce.
Numbers are big bold grotesque numerals stamped inside blocks, counting up with a mechanical tick.
The key moment gets a heavy red ring drawn round it; a wrong result is crossed by two red slabs, a right one by a black tick.
Steps and loops are shown as stations made of different primitives (circle, then square, then triangle) joined by bar arrows; amounts are columns of stacked primary blocks rising one by one.
sound: Wooden block knocks with a little body for every shape set down.
Dry metal taps of type being set for letters, and a crisp numbering-machine clack for counters.
A large paper sheet sliding across a drafting table for each camera track, that halts against a wooden stop.
A small soft wooden marimba for right answers, the key number and the closing line.
avoid: Gradients, drop shadows, rounded corners, outlined shapes or any colour outside the four inks and the paper.
Decorative serif or script type, ornament or hand-drawn wobble; everything is constructed.
Crowded or centred-symmetric layouts that lose the open asymmetric grid.
Clean digital flatness with no print finish; the offset plates and mottle are what make it read as printed.

name: Editorial Data Chart
description: A quality-newspaper data graphic on pale peach paper: bold serif headline, hairline gridlines, one wine-red series picked out against muted greys, labels set right on the lines and handwritten margin notes.
suits: Excellent for numbers, trends, comparisons and evidence-led stories in a calm, credible voice; wrong for playful children's topics, high-energy hype or subjects with no data to show.
look: Flat pale peach paper fills the frame; each panel opens with a thick ink rule across the top that has a short heavier wine block at its left end.
Above the chart: a tiny wine small-caps section kicker, a bold serif headline, a lighter muted serif subhead under it and a small plain note line on units and dates.

Horizontal hairline gridlines only, no vertical lines; the zero line is darker and slightly heavier; value labels sit just above each gridline at the left edge, with the unit written on the top label only.
One highlighted series in wine red with a thicker stroke and a pale wine wash beneath it that fades downward; every other series is a thin warm grey line.
No legend: each series is named directly at its right end, and the highlight's end point is a hollow ring with its name and latest value set beside it.
Forecast or uncertain stretches sit under a faint grey shaded band with a small italic label, and the line turns dashed there.
Annotations are short handwritten notes in ink or muted grey, each joined to its point by a slightly wobbly curved leader ending in a small open arrowhead.
A hairline above a small-caps source line closes the bottom of the frame.
finish: Paper tooth, very light: fine grain at two or three percent that shifts a few times a second so the page feels alive.
Slow push, light: the camera creeps in by one or two percent across a shot; never faster.
Live end point, light: during holds one or two thin wine rings expand and fade from the latest value.
Restraint is the rest of the finish: no textures, glows or shadows beyond these.
motion: The top rule draws across, then the headline and subhead set line by line, each rising a few pixels as it fades in.
Gridlines rule across from left to right, bottom line first, in a quick stagger; tick labels fade in after their lines.
Grey context lines settle in softly, then the highlight line grows from left to right, a small dot leading its tip and the wash filling in behind.
Each handwritten note writes itself on, left to right, once the drawing line has passed its point, then its leader draws to the target.
Scene changes are the page scrolling up to the next panel, like an online long-read; the headline docks into a slim sticky header that lists the sections, with the current one in wine and underlined.
Pace is calm and measured: smooth ease-in-out moves, nothing bounces.
explaining: Every number and series is labelled directly where it is, never through a legend.
Counts are shown as waffle grids of small squares, each square a fixed unit, coloured wine for the focus group and grey for the rest.
Key figures are large serif numerals that count up, with lining figures so digits do not jump.
Emphasis is a hand-drawn ring that overshoots its start like a marker circle, plus the handwritten note explaining why it matters.
Processes are a numbered step strip across the top of the panel and small diagrams drawn in the same hairline style, with nodes as small circles and links as thin lines whose darkness shows strength.
sound: Mouse-wheel notches over a soft, low paper glide when the page scrolls.
A felt-tip pen stroke whose length matches each handwritten note and leader.
Small dry type clicks for counter digits, slowing as the number settles, and one rounder, deeper hit for the key figure.
A very quiet room tone, almost silent, so the hits read.
avoid: 3D charts, heavy gradients, drop shadows, chart borders or boxed legends.
More than one highlight colour, or saturated rainbow series.
Cartoon icons, emoji or playful bouncy motion.
Cluttered labels that overlap; nudge them apart so every label reads cleanly.

name: Kinetic Type
description: A music-video made of words: huge condensed capitals in one acid-yellow ink on near-black, cropped by the frame edges and slamming in on the beat, with outline echoes, glitch slices and one word filled with a dot-screen picture.
suits: Great for punchy, high-energy messages, launches, manifestos and short ideas with a few strong keywords; poor for detailed diagrams, gentle or sensitive topics and anything needing lots of small text.
look: Near-black ground and a single acid-yellow ink; nothing else, every element is either ink or ground.
Words are huge condensed all-caps, scaled so their ink spans the full frame width or a set box, often cropped by the edges, and stacked so the lines touch with no gap between them.
Within a stack the treatments contrast: one word solid, one in outline only, one in a lighter weight beside a heavy one.
One word is stretched unevenly to fill its box and its interior holds a picture made of a 45-degree dot screen (dot size follows brightness), with a thin outline keeping the letters readable.
Tab blocks: a solid yellow rectangle with black letters knocked out of it, sometimes tilted a few degrees.
Filled words carry signatures: thin horizontal speed lines cut out of their lower third, and a band sliced out and shoved sideways with short thin rule ticks beside the cut.
Small captions and labels are bold monospace in inverted tags: yellow box, black text.

palette.role: echo ink (ink at about a fifth strength)

finish: Video grain, light: fine moving grain at about four percent over everything.
Impact shake, medium: on every slam the whole frame jolts a few pixels in a random direction and settles within about a tenth of a second.
Inversion flash, strong but rare: a single frame where ink and ground swap, only on the two or three biggest hits.
Strobe echoes, light: faint outline copies of a moving word fan out behind it and fade.
motion: Everything is locked to a beat grid (about two beats a second): one word or one change lands per beat.
Words arrive hard: punched in with a two-frame squash then held, whipped in from the side trailing echoes, or wiped up from below for tab blocks.
The dot-screen picture inside its word develops dot by dot after the word lands.

Scene changes are a slice-glitch tear (the frame splits into horizontal bands that fly off alternately left and right to reveal the next scene) or a whip-pan where the scene smears off one side with echo copies and the next arrives from the other.
The opening word stack shrinks into a small corner header that stays for the rest of the piece.
explaining: The words themselves do the explaining: the key noun of each beat is set huge and the supporting words smaller beside or above it.
Arrows are heavy straight rules with a solid chevron head, drawn out from their start.
Labels are small mono tags, yellow box with black text, that fall onto their targets.
Numbers are giant condensed numerals that count up fast and land with a slam and, for the key one, an inversion flash.
Charts are solid yellow bars rising one per beat; wrong is a big X of two heavy bars, a loop is a heavy circular arrow.
sound: A low synth pulse on the beat grid underneath, falling silent at every hard cut.
A punchy kick with a bright snap for every word slam, with a detuned synth stab added on the key hits.
A crunchy digital tear for the slice-glitch cut and one fast filtered whoosh for the whip-pan.
Short filtered blips for counter ticks and rising pitched plucks for chart bars.
avoid: A third colour, any gradient, soft glows or photographic images outside the dot screen.
Serif, script or rounded fonts, or lots of small lower-case body text.
Slow fades and gentle easing; motion should hit and stop.
Small words floating in empty space; type should fill and crop the frame.

name: Ink Wash
description: Quiet black-ink brush painting on pale rice paper: a few confident strokes, soft grey washes that bleed outward, lots of empty space and one small red seal.
suits: Suits calm, reflective or contemplative topics such as strategy, nature, process and philosophy; poor for dense data, loud product launches or anything needing bright colour coding.
look: Warm off-white paper with faint long fibres and slight cloudy staining; most of the frame is left empty on purpose, and the subject sits off-centre
Brush strokes swell and thin: a heavy wet press at the start, a tapering tail, with dry-brush gaps where the hair skips over the paper grain at the end
Washes are watery greys that spread past their stroke with a darker rim where the pool dried, layered two or three deep for mountains, mist and shadow
Objects are suggested, not outlined: a few strokes imply a hill, a branch, a roof; bands of pale mist cut the scene into near, middle and far
Ink density is the only depth cue: near things are dark and sharp, far things pale and soft
One accent only: a small square red stamp with a simple carved glyph, placed in a lower corner or beside a key word
Lettering is a slim, upright, high-contrast serif in dark ink, set small and widely spaced, sometimes stacked vertically at the edge
Distinct from Watercolor: no colour mixing and no bright pigments, only black ink in many dilutions
finish: Paper fibre texture laid over everything, soft and low, so the ink seems to sit in the sheet
Wash edges get a slight uneven darkening along the outline and a faint grainy blotch inside, moderate strength
A very light warm vignette at the corners, as if the scroll has aged
Strokes are drawn with tiny wobble in width, never perfectly smooth
motion: Strokes are painted on in real time: the brush travels along the path and the line thickens then thins as it moves
Washes bloom in slowly, spreading outward from the stroke over a second or two, then settle
Beats change by fading mist across the frame; the old scene thins to pale grey as the next one emerges
Pace is slow and unhurried, with long still pauses after each stroke group
Nothing bounces or snaps; the red seal simply presses down with a quick soft squash and stays
explaining: Keys words are written in a few brush characters or a single sweep of the brush, next to their subject, never in boxes
Arrows are single curved brush sweeps with a ragged dry tail and a small pressed-in head
Numbers are large, written in dark ink as ordinary lettering, with a pale wash blot behind to anchor them
